summary: A 1974 note describing proposed changes to the ARPANET IMP and the way hosts connect to it. It covers decoupling the message numbering of different hosts, host-to-host access control, a message number window, and handling messages outside the normal mechanism. It points to BBN Report 1822 for the interface itself.

plainLanguage.summary: The ARPANET's message routers needed new rules for how computers talk to them. This note suggests keeping each computer's message counting separate and adding some access checks.

subtitle: Four planned changes to the ARPANET IMP software and the IMP/Host interface, announced by BBN in October 1974.

tldr.problem: All pairs of hosts on two IMPs shared just four outstanding messages, so hosts could interfere with each other, and there was no host-to-host access control or way to send messages outside the normal message-number mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The IMP software gets separate message number sequences per pair of hosts drawn from a pool, an access check, a window of eight instead of four, and a new single-packet message type 3 that bypasses the ordered, error-controlled path.
tldr.outcome: BBN states all changes are backward compatible with possible minor exceptions in timing. Users were asked to file the note with BBN Report 1822 until that document is updated.

facts.label: Access check interval
facts.value: After two minutes of no communication

sections.title: Announcing Four Changes
sections.content:
RFC 660 announces that in the next few weeks several changes will be made to the IMP software, including changes to the IMP/Host software interface specified in BBN Report No. 1822. They come in four areas: decoupling of host message number sequences, host-to-host access control, expansion of the message number window from four to eight, and messages outside the normal message number mechanism.

All changes are said to be backward compatible with possible minor exceptions in timing.
sections.plainLanguage: BBN, the group that built the network boxes, is telling everyone about four upgrades that are coming soon.

sections.title: Separate Message Numbers and a Wider Window
sections.content:
Since 1972 the IMP system has allowed exactly four messages outstanding between any pair of IMPs, shared by every pair of hosts on those two IMPs, so hosts could interfere with each other. The IMP's message number logic will change to give a separate sequence between each pair of hosts.

To keep storage manageable, the host-to-host sequences come dynamically from a limited pool, sized so it seldom interferes. No hosts are prevented from communicating: if the pool would be exhausted, it is multiplexed in time among the conversations, so all may be slowed but none stopped.

Once sequences are per pair of hosts, the number of messages allowed outstanding between a pair grows from four to eight, permitting increased throughput in some cases.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, everyone at one post office shared four mail slots, so they got in each other's way. Now each pair of friends gets its own slots, and eight at a time.

sections.title: Host-to-Host Access Control
sections.content:
Upon instructions from ARPA, the IMPs get a mechanism that checks, using bits in the IMP, that a pair of hosts has administrative permission to communicate. The check is normally made whenever a pair attempts to communicate after not having communicated for two minutes.

If the pair is not allowed to communicate, a special type of Destination Dead Message (sub-code 3) is returned to the source host. Initially the default is to allow all hosts to communicate with each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The network can now keep a list of who is allowed to talk to whom. If you are not on it, you get a polite "no" message back.

sections.title: Messages Outside the Normal Mechanism
sections.content:
For limited experiments, specified hosts may communicate outside the normal ordered, error-controlled sequences. A single-packet message from a host to its IMP with a new message type, 3, goes directly into the store-and-forward logic marked as special. A multi-packet message of type 3 is discarded.

These packets are routed normally, possibly arriving out of order, and at the destination IMP are put directly on the host output queue, skipping reassembly, marked with a new IMP-to-host message type, also 3. There is no retransmission, reassembly, RFNMs or incomplete transmissions, and a message is discarded if network resources are insufficient. The normal mechanism stays intact for everything else.

Because uncontrolled use would degrade the network for all users, the set of hosts allowed to use this mechanism is regulated by the Network Control Center.
sections.plainLanguage: This is like a fast lane for notes with no receipt and no promise they arrive in order. Only a few approved computers may use it, because too many notes would clog the roads.
